Compute the conditional AIC of fitted isoscapes

Source: R/AIC.R
AIC.ISOFIT.Rd

This function computes the conditional AIC (cAIC) of the isoscape models fitted with isofit or isomultifit, corrected for the number of parameters estimated in the residual dispersion model. This corrected cAIC measures the ability of the joint fit of the mean model and of the residual dispersion model to predict the isotopic values observed at the source locations. It thus allows for the comparison of isoscape models differing not only in the structure of their mean model but also in the structure of their residual dispersion model.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'ISOFIT'
AIC(object, ..., k = 2)

Arguments

object

The output of a call to isofit or isomultifit.

...

Optionally, more fitted objects created by isofit or isomultifit.

k

The penalty per parameter, which must be equal to 2 (the default) since the cAIC computed by spaMM does not allow for other values. This argument only exists for consistency with stats::AIC.

Value

If a single fitted object is provided, the corrected cAIC (a numeric value). If several fitted objects are provided, a data.frame with one row per object and the following columns: the number of parameters estimated in the mean model (K_mean) and in the residual dispersion model (K_disp), the cAIC of the mean model before correction (cAIC_uncorrected) and the corrected cAIC (cAIC).

Details

For linear mixed models whose residual errors have a variance (or covariance) depending on \(r\) unknown parameters, Overholser & Xu (2014, theorem 1 and equation 6) showed that the plug-in estimate of the cAIC is \(-2 \log L_c + 2 (\textrm{tr}(H) + r)\), where \(\log L_c\) is the conditional log-likelihood and \(\textrm{tr}(H)\) is the effective number of degrees of freedom of the fixed and random effects (the trace of the "hat" matrix). The cAIC computed by spaMM for the mean model (mean_fit) is \(-2 \log L_c + 2 \textrm{tr}(H)\): it treats the residual variances (pred_disp) as known, while they have been predicted from the fit of the residual dispersion model (disp_fit). Following Courtiol & Rousset (2017), we thus add the missing term by considering the parameters estimated in the residual dispersion model (K_disp) as the parameters of the residual variance of the mean model (i.e. \(r = K_{disp}\)):

$$cAIC = cAIC_{mean\_fit} + 2 \times K_{disp}$$

K_disp is the number of fixed-effect coefficients, plus the number of random-effect variances, plus the number of parameters of the Matérn correlation function (including the nugget, if any), plus the number of residual dispersion parameters that have been estimated in disp_fit (see spaMM::DoF). Parameters kept fixed during the fit (e.g. the residual variance of disp_fit, which is fixed to its theoretical expectation) are not counted.

For a fit produced by isomultifit, the cAIC is the sum of the corrected cAIC of all the pairs of models (one per strata), since all pairs are fitted independently on non-overlapping data. Similarly, K_mean and K_disp are summed over all pairs.

As for any information criterion, only models fitted on the same data can be compared. The lower the cAIC, the better the predictive power of the fitted isoscape. Since the goal of an isoscape is prediction, there is no need to favour simpler models beyond what the cAIC already accounts for. Note, however, that the cAIC only reflects the quality of the predictions at the source locations, so always check the isoscapes produced by the selected model (e.g. by plotting the prediction variance; see isoscape).

This correction should be seen as an approximation. First, the result of Overholser & Xu (2014) is asymptotic and the plug-in cAIC can be biased in small samples (they also discuss alternative corrections for small samples). Second, their result assumes that the parameters of the residual variance are estimated jointly with the other parameters of the model, whereas IsoriX estimates them in a separate fit (disp_fit). Third, the residual variances predicted by disp_fit also depend on the predicted values of its random effects, which are not counted in K_disp. Finally, the cAIC has been shown to tend to favour models with additional random effects (Greven & Kneib 2010; Overholser & Xu 2014), so comparisons of models differing in their random-effect structure should be interpreted with care.

References

Courtiol, A., Rousset, F. (2017). Modelling isoscapes using mixed models. https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/207662v1

Greven, S., Kneib, T. (2010). On the behaviour of marginal and conditional AIC in linear mixed models. Biometrika, 97(4):773-789. doi:10.1093/biomet/asq042 .

Overholser, R., Xu, R. (2014). Effective degrees of freedom and its application to conditional AIC for linear mixed-effects models with correlated error structures. Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 132:160-170. doi:10.1016/j.jmva.2014.08.004 .

Examples


## The examples below will only be run if sufficient time is allowed
## You can change that by typing e.g. options_IsoriX(example_maxtime = XX)
## if you want to allow for examples taking up to ca. XX seconds to run
## (so don't write XX but put a number instead!)

if (getOption_IsoriX("example_maxtime") > 20) {
  GNIPDataDEagg <- prepsources(data = GNIPDataDE)

  ## Fitting two isoscape models differing in their residual dispersion model
  GermanFit1 <- isofit(
    data = GNIPDataDEagg,
    mean_model_fix = list(elev = TRUE, lat_abs = TRUE)
  )

  GermanFit2 <- isofit(
    data = GNIPDataDEagg,
    mean_model_fix = list(elev = TRUE, lat_abs = TRUE),
    disp_model_fix = list(elev = TRUE)
  )

  ## Corrected cAIC of a single fit
  AIC(GermanFit1)

  ## Comparison of the two fits
  AIC(GermanFit1, GermanFit2)
}
